entities.name: Raimondo Guglielmo des Fargues
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Raimondo Guglielmo des Fargues, born in Gascony, France, emerged as a pivotal figure in the early Avignon Papacy, serving as a Cardinal-Deacon from 1310 until his death on October 13, 1346. His significance stems primarily from his familial connection to Pope Clement V, his uncle, which propelled him into the highest echelons of the Roman Catholic Church at a time of profound institutional change. Des Fargues's career spanned the reigns of three Avignon Popes—Clement V, John XXII, and Benedict XII—making him a witness and participant in the consolidation of papal power in Avignon and the complex political maneuvering between the papacy, the French monarchy, and other European powers during the tumultuous 14th century. His extensive benefices, including the Archdeaconry of Leicester in England, underscore the widespread influence and fiscal reach of the Avignon curia.

Elevated to Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria Nuova on December 19, 1310, by his uncle Clement V, des Fargues quickly became an influential voice within the College of Cardinals. He played a direct role in the papal elections, participating in the protracted Conclave of Carpentras/Lyon (1314–1316) that eventually elected Pope John XXII, and again in the Conclave of 1334 that chose Pope Benedict XII. His tenure saw the papacy's deepening administrative reforms, the suppression of the Knights Templar, and the ongoing theological disputes that characterized the era. Despite his French origins and strong ties to the Avignon court, his holding of the Archdeaconry of Leicester from 1310 to 1346 illustrates the international nature of ecclesiastical appointments and the flow of church revenues across national boundaries, even amidst growing Anglo-French tensions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Raimondo Guglielmo des Fargues's three-decade tenure as a cardinal provided continuity and influence during the critical early years of the Avignon Papacy, participating in two papal conclaves and managing significant international benefices. His career exemplifies the intertwined political and spiritual power of the curia before the Black Death and the Western Schism.
